rewrites.686DD6D2: No single source measures demand for the province, so this section triangulates. Sources count different things (arrivals, trips or passengers), cover different places (city, province or country) and use different methods (surveys or aviation records). The demand work combined Stats SA, Wesgro and global datasets. It anchored its projections on aviation schedule data and the traveller survey, with simplifying assumptions it does not list. The national Department of Tourism adds two cautions. Airport passenger and card data include non-tourists and can overstate volumes or spend. Spend, trip length and provincial spread come only from SA Tourism's departure survey, not from border counts.[^70]
rewrites.78A7D7F2: Length of stay is a growth lever in its own right, and its measures disagree. SA Tourism's departure survey puts the average international tourist's stay in the Western Cape at 12.5 nights in 2025, against 14.8 nationally and 13.0 in the province in 2023. Mobile-location data puts international tourists at 2.9 days in Cape Town in 2025 and 3.0 in 2023, when 31.5% stayed one day. The survey bands in the Demand-Side Analysis show 5% staying 1 to 2 days, 12% staying 3 to 4 and 14% staying 7 to 10, on bands that sum to 48%.[^77]
rewrites.5E1CAC34: Each added night raises spend and regional reach without an added seat or a peak-hour runway slot. Three levers follow. Extensions can be sold through the safari and tour operators who build the itinerary, with the Cape Winelands, the Whale Coast and the Garden Route as the second leg (objectives 5 and 10). Business-event delegates can add nights before or after an event (objective 2). Singapore's work to turn transit into stays shows a hub pursuing the same gain (section 2.2). The plan tracks average nights in the province by market group as indicator T2-30, with a baseline set from SA Tourism data in 2027.
rewrites.2F6097D7: Stakeholders describe the same travellers from the product side. SATVITO sees an opening with cultural travellers if the province packages its cultures, township and village experiences included. CapeNature finds its international appeal concentrated in eco-adventure niches such as hiking and bouldering, and the Overberg District reports rising demand for remote experiences. Both fit the two segments named for the regions and the green season.[^84]
rewrites.5D886C22: Concentration is not new. The same five markets held 61% on the Cape Town overseas air-arrivals basis for January to August 2024, with the UK and the USA at 18% each and Germany at 15%. The growth markets remain small: India supplied about 2.6% of South Africa's overseas tourists in September 2025, the Middle East 2.3% and China 1.4%.[^86]
rewrites.21F627C5: Within the five, the USA is gaining. Its share rose 3.8 points on 2019, to 15.0% in 2024, on the Provincial Treasury's count of all international arrivals at Cape Town International, Africa included. The UK's and Germany's shares slipped by under a point and France's fell 1.6 points. That count is wider than the overseas shares above.[^87]
rewrites.7B6086CE: Two other counts are lower and rank the markets differently. The Provincial Treasury's 2024 regional averages put Middle East visitors first, at R23,900, then Europeans at R19,900, with North Americans at R16,100 against R17,000 for all international tourists. SA Tourism's 2025 departure survey, as Wesgro Research reports it, gives R22,900 for the UK, R20,500 for Germany and R16,600 for the USA. This report uses the Demand-Side Analysis figures because they are by country for 2024, though their basis is not stated. On all three counts Europe spends more than most, so the Western Cape must hold yield in its mature markets, Europe first, while volume growth comes from elsewhere.[^89]
rewrites.5B4606F5: Most of these visitors arrive through someone else's hub. The UAE route carried 222,923 air arrivals into Cape Town in 2025, Qatar 126,078, Ethiopia 123,250 and Turkey 89,090. Together these four hub routes held 53% of arrivals on the ten largest routes (section 2.1). The hubs, not the source markets, are the province's working gateways.[^90]
rewrites.3536065B: Demand peaks in the southern summer. In 2025, 12.7% of overseas visitors travelled in December, 11.5% in January and 11.3% in November, against 6.1% in June and 6.5% in August. October to March together account for about 62% of the year once the twelve reported shares, which sum to 104.9%, are scaled to 100%.[^91]
rewrites.3DDCF3F5: Source: 2024: Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p25 and p32 (Wesgro Visitor Tracking Survey 2024; shares sum to 100%). 2025: Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p12 (Stats SA and SA Tourism 2025; the printed shares sum to 104.9%, and the October to March share is computed with the 2025 shares normalised to 100%).
rewrites.06C42315: Supply follows the same curve. June carries 6.4% of 2025 international seat capacity into Cape Town, and airlines cut seats across the green season. Growth depends on converting more interest into visits from April to September, not on pushing more demand into the peak months. Filling those months needs seats as well as conversion (section 2.4).[^93]
rewrites.70459508: The green season has grown faster than the peak over the decade, but not lately. April to September carried 38.7% of the year's international and regional passenger movements in 2015, 41.4% in 2019 and 41.6% in 2023. The share then eased to 41.1% in 2024 and 40.8% in 2025. Since 2019 the green months have grown 24.4% and the other six months 27.8%. Volume is rising; the balance is not.
rewrites.76A78ADB: Green-season traffic has doubled since 2015, and its share of the year rose to 41.6% in 2023 before easing.
rewrites.3EB4D4F8: On the third lever, section 2.4 sets out the 1.8 million seat marker and what the target requires. The model gives no load factor, penetration rate or seat table, so its levers can be read but not recomputed (Appendix A2).[^97]
rewrites.6C6404C6: The demand work traced three growth markets from inspiration to the visit itself and assessed how each reaches Cape Town. Its findings are qualitative. It gives no platform shares, booking lead times or sources and maps no mature or African market. Demand from India and China also weakened in 2026 (above), despite pilot access to the Electronic Travel Authorisation before its August 2026 launch (section 2.5).[^107]
rewrites.45AE64CF: No direct service links China and Cape Town. The hub volumes given are 8,593 passengers through Dubai, 6,853 through Addis Ababa, 6,728 through Singapore, 5,398 through Doha and 1,443 through Johannesburg, with no year or source. A China Southern service from Guangzhou is the likeliest first direct route. Until one comes, Wesgro should treat China as a long-term investment in awareness and indirect volume.[^109]
rewrites.14C99F43: India is among Cape Town's largest unserved air markets. Addis Ababa and Dubai carry 81% of Indian travellers, and half of them start in Mumbai. The hub volumes given are 30,184 through Addis Ababa, 28,621 through Dubai, 8,660 through Doha and 1,099 through Johannesburg. Direct service is unlikely before 2030, because of aircraft constraints at Air India and IndiGo, and none is committed. Bilateral air rights sit with national government, so Wesgro should build early relationships with the Indian carriers and authorities.[^111]
rewrites.2ECBEC67: Each market meets a readiness gap once it looks closer: little Mandarin service, few visible vegetarian options or Indian-language guides and no Arabic-language booking or local-currency pricing. Section 2.1 sets these gaps among the six barriers, and visas sit with national government (section 2.5).[^114]
rewrites.6038E8A2: The province's own channels also lag. The Department of Economic Development rates destination platforms behind international practice in online presence and AI adoption. The Overberg says its proximity to Cape Town is not packaged before travellers book flights, and SATVITO finds that township and village businesses need stronger digital positioning. Google reports that market-level search data can show which overseas markets already look for the Western Cape. Yet most of its tourism analysis is national, and data specific to the province is unconfirmed. Information about the province belongs where each market searches and decides, through creators, agents and booking platforms, not in broad campaigns alone.[^115]
rewrites.6F3CD562: Stakeholders see the same gap between pool and visits. The Cableway describes the rest of Africa as largely untapped, with regional travellers stopping in Johannesburg. The CTICC reports that visa requirements and tight budgets hold back African event demand. Africa is both a foundation to keep and a source of high-spending visitors to grow.[^119]
rewrites.4A5AF6E4: Regional spread does not need the main event to move. Cape Town stays the base for international conferences and large exhibitions, limited by peak-season hotel availability and transport pressure. Stellenbosch, with its university and conference base, and George, with its airport, are credible secondary hubs that can take delegates' extra nights. The Overberg District reports group demand beyond its venues, and Mossel Bay lacks a branded hotel able to host conferences. The lever needs one events calendar, as Melbourne has (section 2.2), bids aimed at May to August and a measure for each type of buyer.[^126]
rewrites.61B9EDA8: Three messages run through the summary statements. Growth should go to under-visited regions and the green season, not to flagship sites under pressure, yet activation is too weak to smooth demand. Marketing and digital capability lag international practice, and destinations do not package proximity and itineraries before travellers book flights. The mature markets remain the base but have had too little international marketing, while activation in India, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific is too thin to turn early interest into visits.[^128]
rewrites.33123493: Goal 1 must convert interest into visits, fill the green season, win growth markets on the routes and platforms they already use, hold yield in mature markets and build the African base. Seats, regional product and the enabling environment (sections 2.4 and 2.5) decide whether that demand lands.
rewrites.56A71751: **Objective 4, Convert India and China hub traffic.** About 101,000 hub journeys a year reach Cape Town, and a direct Indian route is unlikely before 2030. The model has both markets more than doubling by 2035, yet national arrivals from both fell in the first nine months of 2026. On SA Tourism's count, fewer than three in ten Indian or Chinese visitors to South Africa reach the province.
